key_insight: A flat plate generates excess drag during reversal because it re-encounters its own wake, and this wake-capture effect is mainly controlled by how far it traveled before turning around.
engineering_relevance: For flapping-wing and reciprocating mechanisms, pre-reversal stroke length strongly affects transient force spikes, so wake interaction must be included beyond quasi-steady drag models.
method: Tested forward-and-back translation of a flat plate at insect-flight-relevant Reynolds numbers.
Compared measured reversal-phase drag against quasi-steady predictions to isolate excess drag.
Interpreted wake interaction using flow observations and a point-vortex model for the starting vortex ring.
evidence_signal: The abstract reports measured excess drag during reversal, with force traces and wake velocity decay changing systematically with pre-reversal travel distance and with distinct peaks when the starting vortex detaches and reforms.
watch_item: The point-vortex scaling is a simplified model, so its predictive accuracy may be limited when wake geometry, vortex shape, or Reynolds-number effects depart from the studied regime.
paper_title: Reversal of a flat plate into its wake: a minimal model for wake capture
